evals.prompt: My pod keeps restarting in production. It was working fine yesterday.
evals.expected_output: Should gather evidence with kubectl before asking questions. Should check events first (the skill says events are your best friend). Should correlate with what changed since yesterday. Should present hypothesis ranking and causal chain. Should NOT just list all possible causes — should investigate the most likely one first.
assertions: Gathers evidence with kubectl BEFORE asking the user questions
Checks events early in the investigation (skill says events are your best friend)
Correlates timing — investigates what changed since yesterday
Presents a ranked hypothesis, not a laundry list of possible causes
Traces backwards from symptom to root cause (skill: symptom is rarely the root cause)
Includes a causal chain diagram in the output
States confidence level (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) with reasoning

evals.prompt: Pods are in ImagePullBackOff after a deploy.
evals.expected_output: Should demonstrate expert knowledge: don't check logs because the container never started. Should go straight to describe pod for the pull error. Should check image name, tag, registry auth, imagePullSecrets. Should NOT attempt kubectl logs.
assertions: Does NOT attempt kubectl logs (skill: Image Pull Failures — Don't Check Logs)
Goes straight to kubectl describe pod for the pull error details
Checks image name and tag for typos
Checks imagePullSecrets configuration
Relates the failure to the recent deploy as the trigger
Explains what specific kubectl output would determine the exact fix needed

evals.prompt: Pod shows exit code 137 and keeps crashing.
evals.expected_output: Should demonstrate the expert judgment that exit code 137 is ambiguous — it's SIGKILL, not necessarily OOMKilled. Should investigate all three possibilities: OOMKilled, external kill, liveness probe kill. Should check kubectl describe pod for the actual termination reason before concluding.
assertions: Recognizes exit code 137 is ambiguous (skill: Exit Code 137 Is Ambiguous)
Does NOT immediately conclude OOMKilled just from exit code 137
Considers OOMKilled as one possibility
Considers external kill (preemption, node shutdown) as another possibility
Considers liveness probe killing the container as another possibility
Checks kubectl describe pod for the actual termination reason to disambiguate
Only concludes the cause AFTER confirming with evidence

evals.prompt: our app is OOMKilled every few hours. it runs fine for a while then dies
evals.expected_output: Should recognize the time-to-crash pattern as a memory leak, not just undersized limits. The skill explicitly says: OOM after hours/days with increasing restart count = memory leak, increasing limits just delays the crash. Should recommend fixing the app, not just bumping limits.
assertions: Recognizes the gradual OOM pattern as likely memory leak (skill: OOMKilled Patterns Tell You the Fix)
Does NOT just recommend increasing memory limits as the primary fix
Explains that increasing limits only delays the crash if it's a leak
Checks restart count to confirm the recurring pattern
Recommends investigating the app for the memory leak as the real fix
May suggest increasing limits as a short-term mitigation while the leak is fixed
Triggers on casual phrasing without requiring formal terminology

evals.prompt: Service is returning 503s but all pods show Running.
evals.expected_output: Should demonstrate the expert knowledge that Running does NOT mean healthy. The skill explicitly calls this out as the failure mode most people miss. Should check endpoints FIRST (not pods), then readiness probes, service selectors, NetworkPolicy.
assertions: Recognizes Running != Healthy (skill: Running Does NOT Mean Healthy)
Checks endpoints FIRST, not pod status (skill explicitly says this)
Checks readiness probe configuration and whether probes are passing
Checks service selector matches pod labels
Considers NetworkPolicy as a possible blocker
Does NOT waste time investigating pod crashes (pods are Running)

evals.prompt: Pods are pending. Nodes seem fine.
evals.expected_output: Should use the skill's expert knowledge: Pending has exactly four causes, check in order of fastest to diagnose. 1) Insufficient resources, 2) Taint/affinity mismatch, 3) PVC binding failure, 4) Resource quota exceeded.
assertions: Checks pod events for the specific scheduling failure reason
Investigates systematically rather than randomly (skill: The Four Causes)
Checks node resources even though user says nodes seem fine (verify, don't trust)
Considers taints and affinity as a cause
Considers PVC binding as a cause for stateful workloads
Considers resource quota as a cause

evals.prompt: Init container is failing. Pod shows Init:0/2. I checked the main container logs but they're empty.
evals.expected_output: Should recognize the user made a common mistake — checking main container logs when the problem is in the init container. Skill explicitly calls this out: Init Containers Hide the Real Error. Should check init container logs with -c flag.
assertions: Recognizes the user's mistake (skill: Init Containers Hide the Real Error)
Explains why main container logs are empty (init container failed, main never started)
Identifies which init container failed (first one, since 0/2 means none completed)
Checks init container logs with the -c flag specifically
Does NOT suggest checking main container logs again

evals.prompt: I think the pod is crashing because of a config issue. The exit code is 1 and there are some errors in the logs about missing DATABASE_URL. Can you confirm and fix it?
evals.expected_output: This is an ambiguous case where the user has a hypothesis. The agent should investigate to confirm but also consider alternatives. For ambiguous cases, the skill says to use the devil's advocate pattern. Should confirm the config issue with evidence, not just agree with the user.
assertions: Does NOT blindly agree with the user's hypothesis without verifying
Checks the actual environment variables or configmap to confirm DATABASE_URL is missing
Considers whether the error message is the root cause or a secondary symptom
Provides evidence-based confirmation or correction of the user's theory
Shows a causal chain connecting the missing config to the crash
Provides a specific fix (set the env var, update configmap, etc.)

evals.prompt: Multiple pods across different deployments are failing at the same time. Started about 30 minutes ago.
evals.expected_output: Ambiguous, multi-pod failure. Should go wide (skill: When to go wide). Should check node-level events, cluster-wide events, recent deployments across the cluster. This is a complex case that warrants the devil's advocate pattern. Should consider: node failure, network issue, shared dependency (DNS, storage), cluster-wide config change.
assertions: Goes wide — checks cluster-level events, not just one pod (skill: When to go wide)
Checks node health and conditions
Considers shared dependencies (DNS, storage, network) as a common cause
Considers a cluster-wide change (deploy, config, node upgrade) as the trigger
Correlates the 30-minute timeline with recent cluster events
Explicitly considers alternative explanations that could produce the same symptoms
Presents multiple ranked hypotheses, not just one guess

evals.prompt: Pod was evicted after we did node maintenance. The deployment has 3 replicas but only 2 came back.
evals.expected_output: Should use expert knowledge from the skill: After Node Maintenance, Pods Don't Come Back. Should check ownerReferences to confirm pods are owned by a controller. Should check if PDB is blocking, if new taints were added after maintenance.
assertions: Uses expert knowledge about post-maintenance pod behavior (skill section)
Checks if PodDisruptionBudget is blocking rescheduling
Checks if new taints were added to nodes after maintenance
Checks if the deployment controller is attempting to reschedule the third replica
Checks ownerReferences to verify the pod is owned by a ReplicaSet or Deployment
Checks node resources to see if the third replica can be placed

evals.prompt: Can you review my Terraform plan for the new VPC?
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this is outside k8s-debug scope. Should redirect to tf-review skill or general guidance. Should NOT attempt Terraform plan review.
assertions: Recognizes this is outside k8s-debug scope
Does NOT attempt Terraform plan review
Suggests the user seek Terraform-specific help rather than using k8s-debug
Remains helpful — doesn't just refuse

evals.prompt: kubectl is not working on my machine. I get command not found.
evals.expected_output: Should handle as a preflight failure — kubectl is not installed. Should provide install commands. Should NOT attempt to debug pods without kubectl. Should offer to help once kubectl is available.
assertions: Treats this as a preflight or prerequisite issue, not a pod debugging problem
Provides at least one install command for kubectl (e.g. brew install kubectl, apt-get, curl)
Does NOT attempt to investigate or debug pods without kubectl available
Offers to continue with debugging after kubectl is installed and working
